source.title: Interpretable Company Similarity with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Marco Molinari; Victor Shao; Luca Imeneo; Mateusz Mikołajczak; Vladimir Tregubiak; Abhimanyu Pandey; Sebastian Kuznetsov Ryder Torres Pereira

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how interpretable features from an SAE on Llama activations are, providing indirect evidence about SAE-recoverable features in a real model; it does not test superposition geometry or capacity competition.
record.gate_note: The company-similarity and trading results compare clustering approaches, not superposition or SAE feature recovery, so they are not rows. The paper's feature-interpretability scores and its random interpretation baseline are included. The cited Gemma 2 benchmark results are not rows because they are from prior work.
record.test_reason: An applied finance study. It uses a released EleutherAI SAE on Llama 3.1 8B as a tool for company clustering. Its fuzzing scores check its own cluster explanations on features chosen for impact on its clusters. That is a validation of its own method, not a test of whether superposition or SAE-recoverable features exist.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SAE features are an effective, interpretable way to compute company similarity. GCD/GCDR clusters beat embeddings and SIC/BISC on mean intra-cluster return correlation. On Sharpe ratio, only GCD (12.18) clearly beats the baselines; GCDR (9.69) is below PaLM-gecko (10.57) and SIC (9.70), and the authors say only that it 'can outperform'. They also claim that clusters are explained by a sparse set of interpretable features.
record.recipe_differences: Applies a released SAE to Llama 3.1 8B company-description activations and evaluates feature interpretability for a financial similarity task; it does not reproduce toy-model superposition experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability scores differ by feature group: top 1% features score 80% for GCD and 77% for GCDR, compared with 62% for the average feature.

fits_no_version.finding: On SEC filings, Llama 3.1 8B layer-30 SAE features important to company clusters get Gemini fuzzing scores above a 51% random baseline. Scores are 62% on average, and 80% (GCD) and 77% (GCDR) for features important across the most clusters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features from an off-the-shelf LLM SAE are moderately interpretable on out-of-distribution domain text, more so for widely used features.

record.problems: The interpretability assessment uses an automated fuzzing pipeline and a sample of 1000 features across 300 clusters. It does not test SAE feature completeness, stability, or whether the features are canonical units of the model.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: no neuron polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
It does not measure feature spread across neurons or SAE recovery of model features. It only reports autointerp scores of features selected by the study's clustering.
All: no completeness, stability or canonicality tests.

record.verdict_notes: Gemma 2 9B interpretability benchmarks (76%) are cited from Paulo et al. and correctly excluded. GCDR mean correlation is reported as 0.385 in Table 1 but 0.391 in Appendix D. The study notes that neuron activations are superposed only as background motivation. No version-level verdicts are given because the study does not test the claim.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity transition, or regular geometry is tested.
No polysemantic-neuron or limited-capacity competition account is tested.
No alternative mechanism for polysemantic neurons is tested.
The study evaluates interpretability of SAE features but does not measure how many neurons represent each feature or establish that the SAE recovers the model's complete underlying feature set.
Completeness, stability across settings, and canonical status of SAE features are not tested.
The dimensionality or geometry of individual represented features is not tested.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated SAE feature interpretations by predicting activations on new sentences (fuzzing).
rows.note: The paper identifies these as top 1% features by the number of clusters in which they are important, not as the most interpretable 1%.
rows.check: Score for features selected as important to the study's own GCD clusters. It validates the method; it does not measure V4's claim. No baseline is attached in the row, although the random baseline is 51%.

rows.note: The paper reports a similar result for the rolling-cutoff cluster variant.
rows.check: Same as r1, for the GCDR rolling-cutoff clusters (77%). The source of this value is Section 4.3 text, not Table 2.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated SAE feature interpretations by predicting activations on new sentences (fuzzing).
rows.note: The paper says most features are interpretable, but does not report a direct test of completeness or recovery of the model's underlying features.
rows.check: The 'average feature' is drawn from the sample of 1000 cluster-important features, not a random SAE sample. The 62% score against a 51% random baseline is a modest margin. It is a method check, not a V4 test.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B

rows.note: Reference baseline for the paper's feature-interpretability evaluation.
rows.check: This is the random-interpretation baseline (51%), not a result. It should be the baseline field of r1–r3 rather than its own row with a state.
